steps.explanationAfterStep: Backside attack and loss of bromide in one step. On a primary carbon nothing blocks the approach, so substitution beats elimination with a small base.

title: 1-Bromopropane and ethoxide
subtitle: Primary, small base: substitution wins
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapters 15 and 17

reactants.caption: sodium ethoxide + 1-bromopropane
hintTiers: Is the carbon carrying bromine primary, secondary or tertiary? Is the base small or bulky?
A primary carbon and a small nucleophile: SN2. The oxygen attacks the carbon carrying bromine as bromide leaves. Two arrows.
Ethoxide oxygen lone pair → a new bond to the carbon carrying bromine; the C–Br bond → a lone pair on bromine.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Substitution or elimination? Draw the main pathway.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: E2 is possible, but it is the minor pathway here (about 10%). The carbon is primary and unhindered and ethoxide is small, so it attacks carbon: SN2.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right place to attack. Carbon would now have five bonds: break the C–Br bond at the same time.
A primary carbocation is far too unstable to form on its own. The nucleophile must push bromide out as it attacks: add that arrow.

mechanismSummary: On an unhindered primary carbon a small nucleophile reaches the back of the C–Br bond easily, so SN2 wins: ethyl propyl ether is about 90% of the product. Elimination to propene is the minor pathway.
